label: Sequences
topic: Snowflake Sequences — Semantics, Referencing, GETNEXTVAL, Column Defaults, NOORDER, Altering

questions.stem: What guarantee does Snowflake provide about values generated by a sequence?

options.text: They are globally unique as long as the sign of the interval does not change
They are always contiguous with no gaps
They are assigned in the exact order rows are inserted
They are always positive integers starting from 1

explanation.correct: All values generated by a sequence are globally unique as long as the sign of the sequence interval does not change. Snowflake does not guarantee gap-free or ordered values.

distractors.B: Snowflake explicitly states that generated numbers are not necessarily contiguous — gaps can occur.
distractors.C: There is no guarantee that values are assigned in a particular order, especially with concurrent statements.
distractors.D: Sequences can start from any value and use any step size, including negative values.

questions.stem: Does Snowflake support the currval sequence reference?

options.text: Yes — it returns the last value generated in the current session
Yes — but only within stored procedures
No — Snowflake does not support currval
Yes — but only when used with GETNEXTVAL

explanation.correct: Snowflake does not support currval. The pattern it replaces (single-row inserts for PK-FK relationships) is contrary to Snowflake best practices. Instead, use multi-table INSERT and sequence references in nested subqueries.

distractors.A: currval is not available in any context in Snowflake.
distractors.B: currval is not supported even within stored procedures.
distractors.D: GETNEXTVAL is for generating next values, not retrieving current values.

questions.stem: What does the NOORDER property on a sequence control?

options.text: It specifies that generated values are not guaranteed to be in increasing order
It prevents the sequence from being used in ORDER BY clauses
It removes the gap-free guarantee from the sequence
It randomizes the step size between consecutive values

explanation.correct: NOORDER specifies that the values are not guaranteed to be in increasing order. It can improve performance when multiple INSERT operations are performed concurrently.

distractors.A: NOORDER has nothing to do with SQL ORDER BY clauses.
distractors.C: Sequences never guarantee gap-free values regardless of the NOORDER property.
distractors.D: The step size remains fixed; NOORDER affects the ordering guarantee, not the increment.

questions.stem: Which TWO conditions could cause a sequence to generate duplicate values? (Select TWO)

options.text: Running concurrent queries that reference the same sequence
Changing the sequence interval from positive to negative
Changing the sequence interval from negative to positive
Using the sequence as a column default in multiple tables
Setting the NOORDER property on the sequence

explanation.correct: Changing the interval sign (positive to negative or vice versa) may result in duplicates because the direction reversal can re-generate previously issued values.

distractors.A: Concurrent queries never observe the same value — uniqueness is guaranteed across sessions.
distractors.D: Using a sequence across multiple tables does not produce duplicates; each NEXTVAL call generates a unique value.
distractors.E: NOORDER affects ordering guarantees but does not cause duplicate values.

questions.stem: Which THREE statements about referencing sequences with NEXTVAL are correct? (Select THREE)

options.text: Multiple references to seq.NEXTVAL in the same SELECT produce the same value per row
Each occurrence of seq.NEXTVAL in a query generates a set of distinct values
To get the same sequence value in two columns, use a nested subquery
Sequence values within a single query are always distinct from each other
NEXTVAL can only be used in INSERT statements, not in SELECT
A sequence reference in a query block refers to a specific joined table

explanation.correct: Each NEXTVAL occurrence generates distinct values (unlike some other databases), you must use a nested subquery to share a value across columns, and values within a single query are always distinct.

distractors.A: This is how other databases work, but NOT Snowflake — each NEXTVAL reference produces distinct values.
distractors.E: NEXTVAL can be used in SELECT statements as an expression, not just in INSERT.
distractors.F: A sequence reference in a query block refers to the output of the query block, not any specific joined table.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements about using sequences as column default values are correct? (Select TWO)

options.text: A sequence can be the default for columns in multiple tables simultaneously
Setting a value to DEFAULT in an INSERT triggers sequence generation
Dropping a sequence used as a column default automatically removes the default
A sequence column default prevents explicit values from being inserted
A sequence can only be a default for NUMBER columns in a single table

explanation.correct: A sequence can be referenced as the default for multiple columns across multiple tables, and setting a value to DEFAULT in an INSERT or UPDATE generates a new sequence value.

distractors.C: Dropping a sequence does not remove the default definition — it causes errors when the default is invoked because the identifier cannot be found.
distractors.D: Explicit values can still be inserted into a column with a sequence default.
distractors.E: A sequence can be the default for columns in multiple tables, not just one.

questions.scenario: A team creates a sequence with START = 1 and INCREMENT = 10. The first generated value is 1.
questions.stem: Which range of values is reserved by this first generation?

options.text: Only value 1
Values 1 through 5
Values 1 through 10
Values 1 through 11

explanation.correct: With a step of 10 and generated value 1, the reserved range is 1 to (1 + 10 - 1) = 10 inclusive. The formula is: value to value + (sign(step) * abs(step)) - (sign(step) * 1).

distractors.A: With a step of 10, more than just the single generated value is reserved.
distractors.B: The range extends to value + step - 1, which is 10, not 5.
distractors.D: The upper bound is 10, not 11 — the formula subtracts 1 from the step.

questions.scenario: A developer runs ALTER SEQUENCE seq1 SET INCREMENT = -4 after several inserts. The very next INSERT still generates the old expected next value rather than reflecting the new increment.
questions.stem: What explains this behavior?

options.text: ALTER SEQUENCE requires a warehouse restart to take effect
Snowflake may pre-calculate the next value as soon as the current one is used, so the ALTER may not affect the next operation
The sequence is cached at the session level and requires a new session
ALTER SEQUENCE only affects future sequences, not existing ones

explanation.correct: Snowflake may calculate the next value for a sequence as soon as the current number is used, rather than waiting until the next one is requested. This means ALTER SEQUENCE ... SET INCREMENT might not affect the immediately next operation.

distractors.A: No warehouse restart is needed; the behavior is due to pre-calculation of the next value.
distractors.C: The behavior is not session-level caching but internal pre-calculation by the sequence engine.
distractors.D: ALTER SEQUENCE does affect the existing sequence, just not necessarily the very next value due to pre-calculation.

questions.scenario: A data engineer wants unique sequence values shared across two columns of the same row in a single SELECT statement.
questions.stem: Which approach achieves this?

options.text: Reference seq.NEXTVAL in both columns of the same SELECT
Use the GETNEXTVAL table function and reference its alias in both columns
Use currval after generating with NEXTVAL in the first column
Define a session variable and assign the sequence value before the SELECT

explanation.correct: GETNEXTVAL is a 1-row table function that generates a unique value and joins it to other objects. Multiple columns can reference the alias to share the same generated value.

distractors.A: Each NEXTVAL reference generates distinct values, so the two columns would get different numbers.
distractors.D: Session variables are not the documented mechanism; GETNEXTVAL or nested subqueries are the correct approaches.

questions.scenario: A query uses GETNEXTVAL(seq1) in the FROM clause between tables t1, t2 (before) and t3, t4 (after).
questions.stem: Over which result set are the sequence values generated?

options.text: Over the entire final result of all four tables joined together
Over the result of t1 joined to t2 only, before joining t3 and t4
One value per row of t1 only
One value per row of t3 and t4 combined

explanation.correct: Sequence values are generated over the result of joins between all objects listed prior to GETNEXTVAL in the FROM clause. The resulting rows are then joined to objects listed after.

distractors.A: Values are not generated over the full final result; they apply to the pre-GETNEXTVAL portion.
distractors.C: The generation is over the join of t1 AND t2, not t1 alone.
distractors.D: t3 and t4 are joined after generation; they do not determine the sequence generation scope.

questions.scenario: A sequence with START = 1 and INCREMENT = 1 is heavily used in a high-volume system. The team is concerned about exhausting the sequence's range.
questions.stem: What is the maximum range of a Snowflake sequence value?

options.text: 32-bit signed integer range (-2^31 to 2^31 - 1)
Unlimited — Snowflake sequences have no maximum
128-bit unsigned integer range (0 to 2^128 - 1)
64-bit two's complement integer range (-2^63 to 2^63 - 1)

explanation.correct: A sequence value represents a 64-bit two's complement integer (-2^63 to 2^63 - 1). If the next value exceeds this range, an error results and the query fails.

distractors.A: Snowflake uses 64-bit, not 32-bit, for sequence values.
distractors.C: There is a finite limit; exceeding it causes a query failure.
distractors.D: Snowflake uses signed 64-bit integers, not unsigned 128-bit.

questions.scenario: A team is loading denormalized JSON data and needs to insert into both a people table and a contact table while maintaining PK-FK relationships using sequences.
questions.stem: Which SQL pattern does Snowflake recommend for this?

options.text: Single-row INSERT with currval for the FK reference
INSERT followed by a JOIN to look up the generated PK
MERGE statement with WHEN MATCHED to update the FK
Multi-table INSERT ALL with GETNEXTVAL to share generated keys

explanation.correct: Snowflake recommends multi-table INSERT ALL with sequence references and GETNEXTVAL to generate and share unique keys across related tables in a single bulk operation.

distractors.A: currval is not supported in Snowflake, and single-row inserts are contrary to best practices.
distractors.C: Looking up generated PKs after insert is unnecessary with the multi-table INSERT approach.
distractors.D: MERGE is for upsert patterns, not for the initial normalization of denormalized data.

questions.scenario: A multi-table INSERT uses sequences in both the VALUES clauses and the input SELECT.
questions.stem: Which TWO statements about how generated values behave in this scenario are correct? (Select TWO)

options.text: VALUES clauses referring to a sequence value aliased from the input SELECT receive the same value as the SELECT
VALUES clauses containing a direct seq.NEXTVAL reference receive the same value as the aliased reference
Direct NEXTVAL references in VALUES clauses produce distinct values from the aliased values
In Oracle, sequence references are restricted to VALUES clauses only, whereas Snowflake allows them in both SELECT and VALUES
All sequence references in a multi-table INSERT always produce the same value per row regardless of placement

explanation.correct: VALUES clauses referring to a sequence value aliased from the input SELECT receive the same value. VALUES clauses containing a direct NEXTVAL reference receive distinct values from the aliased ones.

distractors.B: Direct NEXTVAL references produce distinct values, not the same as the alias.
distractors.D: While this is factually true about Oracle, it is not about how generated values behave in Snowflake multi-table INSERT.
distractors.E: Only aliased references share values; direct NEXTVAL references produce distinct values.

questions.scenario: A database is cloned. The original database contains a table with a column that references a sequence for its default value, where both the table and sequence are in the same schema.
questions.stem: Which TWO outcomes occur? (Select TWO)

options.text: The cloned table references the original source sequence
The sequence default is removed from the cloned table
The cloned table references the cloned sequence
The cloned sequence maintains state from the source sequence
The cloned sequence restarts from the original START value

explanation.correct: When the database or schema containing both the table and the sequence is cloned, the cloned table references the cloned sequence. The cloned sequence maintains state from the source.

distractors.B: Source sequences are referenced only when the sequence is outside the cloned scope (different schema/database).
distractors.D: The sequence default is preserved during cloning, not removed.
distractors.E: The cloned sequence does not restart from the original START value; it continues from the source's current state.

questions.scenario: A performance engineer is advising on sequence configuration for a high-concurrency INSERT workload.
questions.stem: Which TWO recommendations improve sequence performance for concurrent inserts? (Select TWO)

options.text: Use the NOORDER property on the sequence
Set INCREMENT = 1 to minimize gaps
Avoid using sequences entirely and rely on AUTOINCREMENT
Use bulk INSERT statements rather than single-row inserts
Set a large negative INCREMENT to reduce contention

explanation.correct: NOORDER can improve performance when multiple INSERT operations are performed concurrently by relaxing ordering guarantees. Bulk inserts are also recommended over single-row inserts for Snowflake best practices.

distractors.B: Setting INCREMENT = 1 does not improve performance; the gap concern is irrelevant since gaps are expected.
distractors.C: AUTOINCREMENT uses sequences internally; the performance characteristics are similar.
distractors.E: A large negative increment does not reduce contention; it changes the direction of value generation.

questions.scenario: A developer places GETNEXTVAL(seq1) between t1,t2 and t3,t4 in a FROM clause and is confused by the join behavior.
questions.stem: Which THREE statements about GETNEXTVAL placement in FROM clauses are correct? (Select THREE)

options.text: GETNEXTVAL must be aliased to reference the generated values
The order of objects in the FROM clause does not matter when GETNEXTVAL is present
There is an implicit lateral dependence between GETNEXTVAL and all other objects in the FROM clause
Joins may not reorder around GETNEXTVAL
GETNEXTVAL generates values over the full Cartesian product of all tables
Multiple GETNEXTVAL calls in one FROM clause are prohibited

explanation.correct: GETNEXTVAL must be aliased, there is an implicit lateral dependence between it and all other FROM objects, and joins may not reorder around GETNEXTVAL — this is an exception in SQL where object order matters.

distractors.B: The order of objects DOES matter when GETNEXTVAL is present — it determines what the sequence generates over.
distractors.E: Values are generated over the pre-GETNEXTVAL portion only, not the full product.
distractors.F: Multiple GETNEXTVAL calls can appear in a single FROM clause (the normalization example uses two).

questions.scenario: A team wants to understand what happens when the internal representation of a sequence's next value exceeds the 64-bit range.
questions.stem: Which TWO outcomes or remediation steps apply? (Select TWO)

options.text: The sequence wraps around to the START value automatically
An error results and the query fails
The fix is to use a smaller increment value or create a new sequence with a smaller start value
Snowflake automatically extends the range to 128 bits
The sequence silently starts producing NULL values

explanation.correct: If the next value exceeds the 64-bit range, an error results and the query fails. The fix is to either use a smaller increment value or create a new sequence with a smaller start value.

distractors.A: Sequences do not wrap around; they error when the range is exceeded.
distractors.D: Snowflake does not automatically extend the integer range.
distractors.E: Sequences produce errors, not NULL values, when the range is exceeded.

questions.scenario: A sequence has START = 100 and INCREMENT = -5. The first generated value is 100.
questions.stem: Which range of values is reserved by this first generation?

options.text: Values 95 to 100
Values 96 to 100
Values 100 to 105
Values 100 to 104

explanation.correct: With step -5 and value 100: reserved range = value + (sign(-5) * abs(-5)) - (sign(-5) * 1) = 100 + (-5) - (-1) = 96 to 100 inclusive.

distractors.A: The formula yields 96 as the lower bound, not 95.
distractors.C: With a negative step, the reservation extends below the value, not above it.
distractors.D: This would apply to a positive step of 5 (100 to 104), not a negative step.

questions.scenario: A developer drops a sequence that is used as the default expression for a column in an existing table. They then attempt to insert a row without specifying that column.
questions.stem: What happens?

options.text: The column receives NULL because the default is gone
The insert succeeds with a system-generated value
An error is raised saying the identifier cannot be found
The default is automatically removed from the column definition

explanation.correct: If a sequence is named as the default expression of a column and then subsequently dropped, any attempt to insert/update using the default value results in an error saying the identifier cannot be found.

distractors.A: The column does not fall back to NULL; it raises an error.
distractors.B: No system-generated value replaces the dropped sequence.
distractors.D: The default expression is not automatically cleaned up when the sequence is dropped.

questions.scenario: A query generates sequence values using a nested subquery, but some of those values are later filtered out by the outer query's WHERE clause.
questions.stem: What happens to the filtered-out sequence values?

options.text: They are returned to the sequence pool for future use
They are consumed and will not be observed — creating gaps
They are assigned to the next query that references the sequence
The filter prevents the sequence values from being generated at all

explanation.correct: Generated sequence values may not be observed if the associated rows are later filtered out. The values are consumed (creating gaps) and are not recycled.

distractors.A: Snowflake does not recycle or return sequence values to a pool.
distractors.C: Consumed values are never reassigned to subsequent queries.
distractors.D: Nested subqueries generate values before the outer filter applies; the values are already generated.
